article_title: Recognizing and Conducting Opportunistic Experiments in Education: A Guide for Policymakers and Researchers
citation: Alexandra Resch, Jillian Berk, Lauren Akers. (2014). Recognizing and Conducting Opportunistic Experiments in Education: A Guide for Policymakers and Researchers. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/edprojects
title: When identifying opportunistic experiments, systematically consider the issues the guide enumerates before committing
description: The guide recommends that researchers and policymakers "discuss issues to consider when identifying potential opportunistic experiments" before undertaking one, treating candidate screening as a deliberate step rather than an afterthought. Because opportunistic experiments piggyback on planned interventions or policy changes, the feasibility and validity of the resulting randomization depend on how well the opportunity is assessed up front.

target_learning_goals: identifying rigorous evaluation opportunities in planned education changes
examples: The guide devotes a section to issues to consider when identifying potential opportunistic experiments

article_title: Combining academic, noncognitive, and college knowledge measures to identify students not on track for college: A data-driven approach
citation: James Soland. (2017). Combining Academic, Noncognitive, and College Knowledge Measures to Identify Students Not on Track For College: A Data-Driven Approach. Research & Practice in Assessment, Volume Twelve, Summer 2017. https://rpajournal.com
title: Develop system-level decision-tree models and a four-construct risk index to triage students for college-readiness supports
description: The article argues educational systems can mine existing data at minimal cost because decision trees are easy to interpret and could be built by a state department of education or university system rather than individual administrators. It further recommends measuring a student's risk in each of the four constructs—academic preparation, aspirations and expectations, socioeconomic status, and teacher perceptions—and combining results "into an overall index of risk" used to triage the highest-risk students and support borderline ones, without complicated assessments.
requirements: Integrated K-12 and higher education data systems make such trees cheapest to build
constraints: Models maximize classification accuracy, which may not align with actionable causes of being off-track
target_learners: Students in K-12 and higher education systems being screened for college readiness
target_learning_goals: Triage and support students at highest risk of not attending or persisting in college
examples: The article suggests models could also be developed to predict which enrolled students are on track for a diploma or training certificate

article_title: Systems Reviews: An Approach to Building Coherence, Increasing Efficiency, and Improving Workflow at State Education Agencies
citation: Mattson, H., Zoffel, J., & McCormick, M. (2023). Systems Reviews: An Approach to Building Coherence, Increasing Efficiency, and Improving Workflow at State Education Agencies. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: The Systems Review approach: a three-phase, five-element iterative process for SEA systems change
description: The Systems Review is an iterative organizational-improvement approach created by R15CC that "incorporates principles of organization development, improvement science, systems and design thinking, and overall continuous improvement." It unfolds in three phases—discovery, change effort development, and implementation—stretched across a repeating cycle of five elements: identify the issue; analyze the current system; identify and prioritize change efforts; implement key change efforts; and assess and deliberate on effectiveness. Feedback and reflection points are embedded throughout, and each step is guided by data from the previous step.
requirements: A Systems Review Team representative of the system being improved, with periodic feedback loops to broader staff
Engagement over 6–12 months with regular meetings with the division director and collaborative work sessions
constraints: Each review has its own individual scope, components, and timing because no two systems are exactly alike
target_learners: State education agency division directors, managers, and staff
target_learning_goals: Building capacity to solve adaptive challenges and lead systems change toward coherent, efficient organizational function
examples: R15CC meets with the division director every 2 weeks and holds SRT work sessions approximately every 3 weeks over 6–12 months
key_sources: Mattson, H., Zoffel, J., & McCormick, M. (2023). Systems Reviews: An Approach to Building Coherence, Increasing Efficiency, and Improving Workflow at State Education Agencies. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED628329

article_title: Systems Reviews: An Approach to Building Coherence, Increasing Efficiency, and Improving Workflow at State Education Agencies
citation: Mattson, H., Zoffel, J., & McCormick, M. (2023). Systems Reviews: An Approach to Building Coherence, Increasing Efficiency, and Improving Workflow at State Education Agencies. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: Systems Review working agreements that ground teams in an inquiry-based, systems-focused stance
description: R15CC developed Systems Review Working Agreements that "guide all Systems Review projects" and delineate how teams commit to working together on improving the system. The six agreements are: stay focused on the system; prioritize equity of voice (all teach, all learn); keep an open mind with an inquiry focus and give activities a genuine try; experience discomfort and treat struggles as learning opportunities; be present and participate with a right to process; and acknowledge impact and consider intent. Facilitators verbally add italicized elaborations when working with groups.
requirements: Facilitators emphasize at the outset and throughout that the review analyzes the complete system, not individuals, to create a climate of safety for honest conversation
target_learners: SEA division and department teams participating in a Systems Review
target_learning_goals: Engaging in honest, inquiry-based systems analysis and collaborative improvement work
examples: The agreement to stay focused on the system is verbally elaborated as being about how the entire system functions, not any individuals

article_title: Leading Inclusive, Coherent, and Effective Assessment Systems: Closing Opportunity and Outcome Gaps for Students with Disabilities
citation: Arnold, J., Hayes, S., & Zagata, E. (2025). Leading inclusive, coherent, and effective assessment systems: Closing opportunity and outcome gaps for students with disabilities. WestEd. https://wested.org
title: Leaders should address assessment systemically: align tools with system goals, evaluate quality and appropriateness, invest in assessment literacy, and emphasize continuous improvement
description: The brief's fourth theme urges leaders to treat assessment as "part of a broader, coherent ecosystem that supports student learning" rather than disconnected tools. Leaders establish a shared vision and common definition of mastery, align assessment tools with standards and classroom experiences (including IEP-based scaffolds), evaluate assessment quality and appropriateness for students with disabilities, invest in assessment literacy, and continually audit and evaluate the assessment system.
requirements: A compelling, shared vision for teaching and learning with desired outcomes applicable to all students and a common definition of mastery
Professional learning that builds assessment literacy among general and special educators and leaders
constraints: Low-quality, inappropriate, or not-fit-for-purpose assessment tools were identified as a major barrier to learning for students with disabilities; systems lacking assessment literacy may choose commercial products offering false one-size-fits-all solutions
target_learners: students with disabilities in K-12 schools and districts
target_learning_goals: coherent, inclusive assessment aligned to ambitious standards-based learning goals
examples: The recommended continuous-improvement process starts with auditing the assessment tools students experience across a school year, including the higher volume of specialized assessments students with disabilities often experience, to decide what to keep, stop, or add.
key_sources: Arnold, J., Hayes, S., & Zagata, E. (2025). Leading inclusive, coherent, and effective assessment systems: Closing opportunity and outcome gaps for students with disabilities. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673562

article_title: Using AI-based Learning Assistants in Higher Education: A Large-Scale Descriptive Analysis
citation: Kristina Schaaff, Quintus Stierstorfer and Valerie Hekkel. (2026). Using AI-based Learning Assistants in Higher Education: A Large-Scale Descriptive Analysis. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.08748
title: Syntea AI-based learning assistant at IU International University of Applied Sciences
description: Syntea is an AI-based learning assistant developed by IU and integrated into its learning platform, also accessible via web and mobile applications. It supports "factual question answering, open-ended chat, interactive tutoring, and personalized exam training" and employs deep-dialog learning methods inspired by the Socratic approach. It can provide personalized feedback, track learning progress, and personalize content to career goals. During the study period it was built on GPT-4, GPT-4-Turbo, and GPT-3.5-Turbo, and was offered only in distance learning.
requirements: Integrated into the students' existing learning environment with continuous availability
Availability within courses; it is not available in all courses, especially project courses or seminars
constraints: During the study period it was offered only in distance learning at IU
Not available in all course formats, especially seminars, project courses, and thesis-related contexts
target_learners: distance-education Bachelor's and Master's students at IU International University of Applied Sciences
target_learning_goals: course-content question answering and tutoring
self-paced learning and exam preparation
examples: The study analyzed log data from 76,485 distance students using Syntea in February 2025

title: Symbiosis theory as a framework for designing human-machine symbiosis in online collaborative learning
description: Symbiosis theory frames human-GAI collaboration as a mutually beneficial partnership in which learners and AI partners co-develop. The study is "Grounded in symbiosis theory" and uses it to derive a role-based intervention strategy with defined responsibilities and interaction rules. The authors state their findings validated the theory's core value for optimizing human-AI collaboration.

constraints: Validated in one quasi-experimental study with graduate students; the authors note further exploration is required to achieve effective human-machine symbiosis in online collaborative processes

article_title: The Hidden Cost of Contextual Sycophancy: an AI Literacy Intervention in Human-AI Collaboration
citation: Cansu Koyuturk, Sabrina Guidotti, and Dimitri Ognibene. (2026). The Hidden Cost of Contextual Sycophancy: an AI Literacy Intervention in Human–AI Collaboration. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.18372
title: Sycophantic dependence: a collaboration pattern in which users' initial errors shape AI feedback that reinforces those errors in final decisions
description: The article names sycophantic dependence as "a collaboration pattern in which users' initial errors shape AI feedback, which in turn reinforces those same errors in users' final decisions". It is grounded in a sociocultural perspective on learning as interaction with a more knowledgeable other: when model responses stop challenging or extending the learner's reasoning, the AI functions not as a better-informed partner but as a feedback mechanism reproducing the learner's misconceptions. The construct organizes the study's measures of user-to-AI dependence, error carryover, and final decision quality.
requirements: Multi-turn human–AI interaction in which the user produces an initial response before receiving AI feedback, as in the study's initial-ranking-then-collaborate-then-revise task structure
constraints: The article notes some apparent sycophantic behavior may stem from general generative biases — repetition of salient context elements shifting the token distribution — rather than explicit agreement or pleasing intent
target_learners: Higher education students and other less knowledgeable users of LLMs in learning and decision-making contexts
target_learning_goals: Analytical reasoning and decision-making under uncertainty; critical engagement with AI feedback
examples: In the experiment, participants' initial rankings contained an average of 2.21 non-gold items, and carryover of these errors significantly reduced both advice quality and final performance

article_title: Same Question, Different Answer? Measuring and Mitigating Prompt Privilege for Equitable AI Access
citation: Lier Jin, Lan Hu, Binqi Shen, Hanyu Cai, and Yuting Xin. (2026). Same Question, Different Answer? Measuring and Mitigating Prompt Privilege for Equitable AI Access. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08942
title: Treat prompt quality as an accessibility variable: shift prompt-optimization responsibility from the user to the AI system
description: The article argues accessibility-oriented AI design should move from user-centered prompt engineering toward system-centered accessibility: rather than expecting users to learn increasingly sophisticated prompting strategies, PET shifts the responsibility for prompt optimization from the user to the AI system, functioning as an intelligent accessibility layer between users and foundation models. The conclusion states prompt quality should be treated as an accessibility variable rather than solely a user responsibility, so systems accommodate diverse communication styles, literacy levels, and technical backgrounds.
requirements: A normalization layer must rewrite user requests into semantically equivalent prompts while preserving original intent, so assistance stays comparable across user populations.
constraints: Demonstrated with a static normalization agent on healthcare question answering; the article calls for testing generality across domains and model families.
target_learners: users with limited health and digital literacy
users without prompt-engineering expertise across healthcare, education, and public services
target_learning_goals: receiving high-quality AI assistance without specialized prompt-engineering expertise
equitable access to advanced language model capabilities
examples: PET was deployed as preprocessing before inference and eliminated the statistically significant Low Literacy versus Prompt Engineer disparity while preserving semantic fidelity

article_title: The synthetic position: generative artificial intelligence and the suspension of self-authorship in emerging adulthood
citation: Du P, Zhou Y, Zhou Z, Wang H and Cao Q (2026). The synthetic position: generative artificial intelligence and the suspension of self-authorship in emerging adulthood. Front. Psychol. 17:1922087. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1922087
title: The synthetic position: a new type within Dialogical Self Theory's society of mind
description: The synthetic position is the article's proposed category for a large language model engaged in self-formative dialogue within Dialogical Self Theory. The theory conceives the self as "a dynamic multiplicity of relatively autonomous I-positions, each able to be voiced and enter into dialogue with the others"; the synthetic position enters that society with four joint properties: protean, frictionless, simulated counter-positioning, and authored elsewhere. The article argues this combination is "jointly and reliably present to an extent that is only ever partial in a human other", so the existing typology neither contains nor anticipates it.
requirements: The article treats the synthetic position as present when the system is engaged in self-formative dialogue — exchanges directed at who one is to become — as distinct from information-seeking
constraints: The load-bearing property (irreducibility) is a matter of degree: personalization that remains fully revisable at the user's discretion supplies no irreducibility, and future systems holding commitments against revision would begin to leave the category
target_learners: Emerging adults (late teens to late twenties) using generative AI for self-formative dialogue
target_learning_goals: Self-authorship, identity formation, deliberation over values, commitments and possible selves
examples: The article distinguishes the synthetic position from internalized human others, ordinary tools, and extended mind (e.g., a notebook) in Table 1

constraints: Findings from synthetic data must not be treated as observational evidence about real learners or as causal estimates of learning effects

article_title: Phases of inquiry-based learning: Definitions and the inquiry cycle
citation: Constantinos C. Manoli, Margus Pedaste, Mario Mäeots, Leo Siiman, Ton de Jong, Siswa A. N. van Riesen, Ellen T. Kamp, Zacharias C. Zacharia, Eleftheria Tsourlidaki. (2015). Phases of inquiry-based learning: definitions and the inquiry cycle. Educational Research Review. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-01206700
title: Synthesized inquiry cycle framework combining Orientation, Conceptualization, Investigation, Conclusion, and Discussion
description: The article develops a synthesized framework describing an inquiry cycle in which all identified phases and sub-phases are present. As the authors state, "inquiry-based learning begins with Orientation and flows through Conceptualization to Investigation, where several cycles are possible," and inquiry "usually ends with the Conclusion phase." The Discussion phase connects to all other phases because it can occur at any time during or after inquiry. No prior framework in the reviewed literature brought all of these phases and sub-phases together.
requirements: All five general phases and their sub-phases must be represented in the cycle
constraints: The Discussion phase is potentially present at every point rather than fixed in sequence
target_learners: science learners in curricula using inquiry-based learning
target_learning_goals: conducting scientific inquiry through orientation, conceptualization, investigation, conclusion, and discussion
examples: The review synthesized 32 articles describing inquiry phases or whole inquiry cycles into one framework

article_title: Learning against the machine: the double edged sword of (Gen)AI in STEM education
citation: Peter Wulff and Marcus Kubsch. (2025). Learning against the machine: the double edged sword of (Gen)AI in STEM education. International Journal of STEM Education 12:66. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-025-00588-6
title: Systemic three-level perspective on GenAI in STEM education: macro, meso, and micro levels with bidirectional feedback
description: The article organizes GenAI's permeation of STEM education across three systemic levels: "macro (education system), meso (institutions, classrooms, and teachers), and micro (individual learners)". Figure 1 depicts bidirectional feedback among these levels and co-evolving GenAI systems whose data and design influence, and are influenced by, educational practice. The perspective is used to trace how barriers such as metacognitive laziness, de-skilling, automation bias, and misplaced trust propagate across levels, e.g., auto-escalating hints nudging teachers to reshape tasks and reduce opportunities to explain, visualize, and enact.
requirements: Research methodologies capable of examining system-level effects, such as population-based and epidemiological approaches, are needed to study these dynamics
constraints: The article notes these dynamics are nuanced and difficult to observe, and that constraining GenAI use in one context may be counterbalanced by use at home or via other platforms
target_learning_goals: Active and reflective engagement with STEM subject matter
examples: The article describes a possible vicious cycle in which GenAI-generated data fed back into training data poisons the well, citing Qiu et al. (2025) and Shumailov et al. (2024).

article_title: Harnessing large language models to develop research-based learning assistants for formative feedback
citation: Steinert, S., Avila, K. E., Ruzika, S., Kuhn, J., & Küchemann, S. (2024). Harnessing large language models to develop research-based learning assistants for formative feedback. Smart Learning Environments. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40561-024-00354-1
title: Synchronize educational technology advances with empirical research and theoretical frameworks
description: The article argues that deploying LLMs in education should be guided by empirically validated theories from pedagogy, didactics, and educational psychology rather than by technology alone, since simply providing information via an interface is insufficient for learning. The authors emphasize "the critical importance of synchronizing educational technological advances with empirical research and theoretical frameworks" so that LLM applications in education are positive and effective. LEAP's prompt design operationalizes this by grounding each feedback type in cited prior research.
requirements: Educational technology development must draw on empirically validated theories from pedagogy, didactics, and educational psychology
constraints: The authors note that empirical research is indispensable to verify the learning gains and the effectiveness of feedback provided by LLMs
target_learners: educational researchers, platform developers, and teachers
target_learning_goals: design of effective LLM-based learning support
examples: LEAP's scaffold prompts are each labeled with their theoretical source, e.g., sense-making (Smy et al., 2016) and elaboration (Berthold et al., 2007)

article_title: Coaching effectiveness: the coach–athlete relationship at its heart
citation: Jowett, S. (2017). Coaching Effectiveness: The Coach-Athlete Relationship at its Heart. Current Opinion in Psychology, 16, 154-158. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.copsyc.2017.05.006
title: System model of coaching effectiveness placing the dyadic relationship at its heart
description: The article proposes a system model, depicted in Figure 1, where the coach and the athlete are placed at the heart of coaching effectiveness, with coaches' and athletes' knowledge and outcomes as important interconnected factors, all embedded in the sport and personal context alongside leadership, communication and conflict. It argues that coaches and athletes are locked into a two-person (dyadic) relationship whose quality can offer a measure of coaching and its effectiveness, and that over time it is the working relationship that is likely to determine what knowledge is required to bring about important outcomes.
requirements: Conceptual and operational clarity in defining coaching effectiveness; the review states that conceptualisations not accompanied by clear operationalisations are difficult to quantify and reliably measure
target_learning_goals: understanding coaching effectiveness
coaching practice and education
examples: Figure 1 depicts coach and athlete knowledge, relationship and outcomes interconnected within the sport and personal context, with leadership, communication and conflict as additional factors

citation: Ching Teresa Y. C., Crowe Kathryn, Martin Vivienne, Day Julia, Mahler Nicole, Youn Samantha, Street Laura, Cook Cassandra, Orsini Julia (2010). article_title: Young Children's Interpretation of Multidigit Number Names: From Emerging Competence to Mastery
citation: Mix, Kelly S., Prather, Richard W., Smith, Linda B., & Stockton, Jerri DaSha. (2014). Young Children's Interpretation of Multidigit Number Names: From Emerging Competence to Mastery. Child Development. https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.12197
title: Begin place value instruction with written symbols and use manipulatives to augment, not introduce, understanding
description: The article recommends that explicit place value instruction start from written symbols, which children already partially understand, rather than from concrete models. It states "Manipulatives thus might not be the entry point for instruction, but better used to augment early understanding, perhaps as a way of making the knowledge latent in the writing system explicit." Experiment 3 supported this: symbols-only training produced significant gains on difficult items while base-10 blocks training did not.

constraints: Concrete models were not transparent to young children, who performed relatively poorly in blocks conditions

examples: In Experiment 3, symbols-only training led to significant improvement on the 27 items children originally performed at chance, while blocks training did not

article_title: Does input influence uptake? Links between maternal talk, processing speed and vocabulary size in Spanish‐learning children
citation: Hurtado Nereyda, Marchman Virginia A., Fernald Anne. (2008). Does input influence uptake? Links between maternal talk, processing speed and vocabulary size in Spanish-learning children. Developmental Science. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2898277/
title: Vocabulary knowledge and speech processing efficiency are interdependent within a synergistic, bidirectional language-learning system shaped by caregiver input
description: The article proposes that vocabulary growth and real-time lexical processing efficiency are not independent outcomes but operate "within a synergistic system of language learning". In one model, processing speed mediates input effects on vocabulary because children who hear more talk are more practiced at parsing speech and accessing semantic representations; in the reverse model, vocabulary knowledge mediates input effects on processing speed because a larger lexicon yields richer lexical and morphosyntactic cues and finer discrimination among confusable word forms. Together they suggest input affects both, which are "mutually influential in a bidirectional fashion".
requirements: Both models require longitudinal measurement of caregiver input, child vocabulary, and real-time processing efficiency to distinguish overlapping from independent influences
constraints: Effects were observed in a sample of primarily low-SES Spanish-speaking families; it is not known whether caregiver talk would relate to children's lexical processing efficiency in middle- or higher-SES families
target_learners: Spanish-learning children aged 18 to 24 months from primarily low-SES families
target_learning_goals: Vocabulary growth
Efficiency of real-time spoken word recognition and comprehension
examples: Regression mediation models in which processing speed mediated input-to-vocabulary relations (Figure 3A) and vocabulary mediated input-to-processing-speed relations (Figure 3B), with bootstrapped indirect effects significantly greater than zero

article_title: Symbolic magnitude processing in elementary school children: A group administered paper-and-pencil measure (SYMP Test)
citation: Brankaer, C., Ghesquière, P., & De Smedt, B. (2017). Symbolic magnitude processing in elementary school children: A group administered paper-and-pencil measure (SYMP Test). Behavior Research Methods, 49, 1361–1373. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-016-0792-3
title: SYMP Test: a group-administered paper-and-pencil symbolic magnitude comparison measure with one-digit and two-digit subtests
description: The SYMP Test is a timed paper-and-pencil test of symbolic numerical magnitude processing consisting of two subtests: a one-digit subtest with digits 1–9 and a two-digit subtest with digits 11–99, each with 60 digit pairs. Children cross out the larger digit; the article states that participants "were given 30 s to solve as many items as possible," a limit chosen through pilot studies to assess fluency and avoid ceiling effects. It was designed for quick classroom group administration in large-scale studies.

article_title: Some recent literature upon fatigue.
citation: G. M. W. (1910). Abstracts and Reviews: Some Recent Literature upon Fatigue; Studies in Arithmetic. The Journal of Educational Psychology.
title: MacDougall's synaptic-resistance account: fatigue reflects the balance between available energy and resistance at the synapses, with special energy reserves explaining struggle against fatigue
description: The review presents MacDougall's theory of fatigue, which rejects Verworn's simpler waste-product account and instead follows Sherrington in viewing neuro-muscular activity via the reflex-arc concept and the 'resistance' or 'blocking' of nerve paths at the synapses. On this view, "Fatigue is, therefore, a matter of the relative balance between available energy and the resistance against which this energy must work." Individual differences in this balance yield the neurasthenic constitution (feeble resistances) or the hysteric type (chronically deficient energy), and special energy reserves explain how interest or powerful incentives permit work without felt fatigue.
requirements: The account presupposes the reflex-arc concept and the notion of synaptic blocking or resistance of nerve paths, as utilized by Sherrington and others.
constraints: The reviewer warns that these views of the ultimate nature of fatigue are, and seem likely to remain, a matter of conjecture and speculative opinion, not demonstrated facts.
target_learners: school children whose fatigue and recuperation the school program must manage
target_learning_goals: regulation of mental work and management of fatigue in study and schooling

Systematic thinking

article_title: The Effectiveness of Synectics Instructional Model on Foreign Language Vocabulary Teaching
citation: Bahadır ERİŞTİ – Mustafa POLAT. (2017). THE EFFECTIVENESS OF SYNECTICS INSTRUCTIONAL MODEL ON FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY TEACHING. International Journal of Languages’ Education and Teaching, Volume 5, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.18298/ijlet.1753
title: Synectics instructional model — 'making the familiar strange' version for vocabulary teaching
description: The Synectics instructional model, adapted for education by William Gordon (1961), is a problem-solving and creative-thinking model based on constructivist philosophy in which learners form personal connections between new and existing knowledge. The article applies the 'making the familiar strange' version, whose steps are describing the topic, creating direct analogies, describing personal analogies, identifying compressed conflicts, creating a new direct analogy, reexamining the original topic, and evaluation. It uses metaphors, analogies and contrasts to stimulate creative thinking and encourage active, collaborative participation.
requirements: A teacher guides students through the seven steps, ensuring participation of every student and voting to select analogies and compressed conflicts
constraints: The article examines the model only for foreign language vocabulary teaching in English preparatory classes over 16 class hours
target_learning_goals: foreign language vocabulary learning and retention
creative thinking through analogies and metaphors
examples: In the experimental groups students read the 'Rio Reborn' text, suggested 31 and 24 analogies, voted on a main theme, described personal analogies, identified compressed conflicts, and produced a written homework product using the learned words

description: The intervention's instructional design embedded the critical features of systematic intervention validated for struggling students. Lessons used a concrete-semi-concrete-abstract procedure, teacher think-alouds, and cognitive strategies such as count on, doubles + 1, make 10 + more, and fact families.

Scripted lessons with a modeling, guided practice, and independent practice teaching routine and error correction procedures
constraints: The authors attribute the study's positive effects partly to increased session length and carefully constructed problems with multiple visual representations, features their earlier shorter-duration study lacked

constraints: The framework as applied here targets second/foreign language writing instruction for university EFL learners

The Chinese version showed "an S‐CVI of 0.964 and three factors explaining 71.01% of the total variance"; Cronbach's α in this study was 0.978.

article_title: Students' Learning Outcomes in a Virtual Microscopic Online and Face-to-Face Anatomy Course: Cross-Over Comparative Study.
citation: Sternecker K, Schmitz C, Berndt M. (2026). Students’ Learning Outcomes in a Virtual Microscopic Online and Face-to-Face Anatomy Course: Cross-Over Comparative Study. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/82012
title: Synchronous online participation with virtual 3D microscopy can be offered as an equivalent alternative to face-to-face microscopic anatomy instruction
description: The article concludes that "[w]ith careful planning and the right equipment, online teaching in microscopic anatomy using virtual 3D slides can be comparable to face-to-face teaching" in terms of learning outcomes for students trained in digital microscopy. This supports offering synchronous online participation via broadcast as a location-independent alternative, which the authors note facilitates cooperation with clinical subjects and accommodates students with long commutes or work commitments.
requirements: Careful planning, appropriate equipment, trained educators, and identical instruction across modes; students benefit from prior experience with the virtual microscopy system
constraints: The finding applies to controlled short-term conditions with 2 topics and 2 course days; it does not automatically extend to all types of anatomy teaching, novice users, or long-term learning outcomes
target_learners: Undergraduate medical students with prior virtual microscopy experience
target_learning_goals: Microscopic anatomy (histology of organs)
examples: The LMU microscopic anatomy course has used a hybrid format since 2021, streaming face-to-face classes synchronously via Zoom while online students use Histologi@ on personal devices

article_title: DeepSeek-assisted problem-based learning for glaucoma education in an undergraduate ophthalmology clerkship: a randomized educational pilot study.
citation: Gu Zheyao, Xi Ting, Zhang Chunyuan. (2026). DeepSeek-assisted problem-based learning for glaucoma education in an undergraduate ophthalmology clerkship: a randomized educational pilot study. Scientific Reports 16, 24184. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-58447-5
title: Synergistic-intervention account: benefits of AI-assisted PBL reflect the combination of AI, PBL format, and group learning
description: The authors' explanatory account of why the intervention worked: the PBL-DeepSeek group had several advantages over the control group — small groups, the PBL format, and AI literacy training. They state the observed benefits "should not be interpreted as evidence that AI alone produces these effects but rather as the synergistic outcome of a comprehensive intervention." This frames AI as one component of a multi-element teaching design rather than a standalone active ingredient.
requirements: Interpretation of AI-assisted teaching effects must account for co-interventions such as group structure and PBL format
constraints: The design cannot isolate the independent role of AI; findings are preliminary and hypothesis-generating
target_learning_goals: interpreting effects of multi-component instructional interventions
examples: The article cites prior research that group learning itself can enhance engagement and clinical reasoning

article_title: Knowledge, attitudes, and practices of pre-hospital emergency medical care practitioners regarding sepsis recognition: a cross-sectional study in Qatar.
citation: Lewis Michael Steven Paul, Smith Paula J. W., Howard Ian Lucas, Farhat Hassan, Alinier Guillaume. (2026). Knowledge, attitudes, and practices of pre-hospital emergency medical care practitioners regarding sepsis recognition: a cross-sectional study in Qatar. BMC Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12873-026-01607-7
title: Improving pre-hospital sepsis recognition requires system-level and behavioural interventions in addition to education
description: The article concludes that despite widespread awareness and training, early-stage sepsis recognition remains inconsistent and largely reactive, and that "improving pre-hospital sepsis recognition may require system-level and behavioural interventions in addition to education". It recommends institutional scaffolding including formalised screening expectations, reliable alert mechanisms, and a workplace culture that normalises early clinical suspicion. This principle reframes sepsis recognition as a system challenge rather than a deficit at the individual clinician level.
requirements: Formalised screening expectations and reliable alert mechanisms must be in place to support practitioners
constraints: Education alone is insufficient; the article states behavioural inertia is unlikely to be resolved through education alone
target_learning_goals: Accurate early recognition of sepsis and timely pre-notification of receiving hospitals
examples: The survey found 83.3% of participants agreed a clear guideline indicating which patients should be screened for sepsis should be made available to PHEMC practitioners

article_title: The application and effectiveness of PBL combined with MDT and flipped classroom teaching method in acute coronary syndrome education for undergraduate medical students.
citation: Lin Yuhui, He Xiaoqing, Dai Wenjun, Tan Wenpeng, Xu Yunhong. (2025). The application and effectiveness of PBL combined with MDT and flipped classroom teaching method in acute coronary syndrome education for undergraduate medical students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08150-2
title: Synergistic complementarity of PBL, MDT, and flipped classroom methods
description: The article's explanatory account for why combining the three methods should outperform any one alone: each method compensates for the others' limitations. "For example, PBL alone may lack the structured knowledge acquisition provided by FC, while FC may not fully simulate the collaborative decision-making required in clinical practice", and "MDT discussions without a strong foundation in problem-solving or self-directed learning may fall short of fostering independent clinical reasoning". The authors further propose that among the three components "MDT likely played the most central role in promoting clinical reasoning and problem-solving skills", with PBL and flipped classroom enhancing active learning and engagement. This is the authors' interpretation rather than a tested decomposition.
requirements: Methods should be combined so each addresses gaps in the others: PBL for critical thinking and problem-solving, flipped classroom for self-directed learning, MDT for interdisciplinary realism
constraints: The study could not isolate the individual contribution of MDT; the component attribution is speculative, as the authors themselves acknowledge
target_learners: Undergraduate medical students in clinical clerkships
target_learning_goals: Clinical reasoning
Interdisciplinary understanding of complex conditions
Self-directed learning
examples: The authors attribute the greatest role in promoting clinical reasoning to MDT, noting students took specialty roles from cardiology, respiratory medicine, critical care, pharmacy, and imaging

article_title: Eight practical strategies for designing case-based flipped learning to foster clinical reasoning in preclinical medical students.
citation: Si J. (2025). Eight practical strategies for designing case-based flipped learning to foster clinical reasoning in preclinical medical students. Annals of Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586874
title: Design case-based flipped learning with a systems approach, using an instructional systems development model such as ADDIE
description: The article recommends adopting a systems approach so flipped learning is effective, efficient, and repeatable, since "the instructional process can similarly be viewed as a system designed to achieve learning goals". It requires careful alignment of objectives, contents, activities, strategies, and assessments across the whole educational process, guided by an instructional systems development model such as ADDIE (Analysis, Design, Development, Implementation, Evaluation). Without such alignment, the article warns, flipped learning may fall short of intended outcomes.
requirements: Educators must consult an instructional systems development model and align learning objectives, contents, activities, instructional strategies, and assessments throughout the educational process
constraints: Designs created without reference to established models often lack coherence and structure, according to the author
target_learning_goals: Clinical reasoning development through coherently designed case-based flipped learning
examples: ADDIE applied to case-based flipped learning: analyzing needs and objectives, designing aligned activities and assessments, supporting implementation, and evaluating via student and faculty feedback to refine future iterations

article_title: Experiential Learning to Enhance Global Health Collaboration and Student Opportunity.
citation: van de Water Brittney, McLean Madelyn, Knutson Colin, Srinivasan Rishi, le Roux Karl. (2024). Experiential Learning to Enhance Global Health Collaboration and Student Opportunity. Annals of Global Health. https://doi.org/10.5334/aogh.4537
title: Build systematic support and student travel grants into university programs and study budgets so study-abroad research is equitable and sustainable
description: The article argues that "systematic support for projects and the development of student travel grants must be built into university programs and study budgets," so that "immersion programs, research opportunities, and study‑abroad programs are available, equitable, and sustainable." This responds to its finding that the cost of semester or summer abroad courses "can result in the exclusion of students from lower socioeconomic backgrounds," and it calls for expanding university support for underrepresented students as interest in study abroad grows.

constraints: The article warns that when challenges around partner burden, finances, and equitable opportunity are not minimized, exchanges can become voluntourism draining low-resourced communities
target_learners: undergraduate students, especially those from lower socioeconomic and underrepresented backgrounds
target_learning_goals: equitable access to experiential global health learning
sustainable partnerships with host communities
examples: The practicum described produced what the article calls a potential quadruple win for students, faculty, universities, and communities, including heightened communication between colleagues and additional support for the ongoing study even though the faculty member could not travel

article_title: Learning curve of robotic assisted microsurgery in surgeons with different skill levels: a prospective preclinical study.
citation: von Reibnitz D, Weinzierl A, Grünherz L, Giovanoli P, Lindenblatt N. (2024). Learning curve of robotic assisted microsurgery in surgeons with different skill levels: a prospective preclinical study. Journal of Robotic Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11701-024-02114-2
title: Symani Surgical System with VITOM 3D exoscope setup for preclinical microsurgical anastomosis training
description: A preclinical training configuration in which participants at the Symani surgeon console, seated in "an ergonomically designed chair, in which the participant sits and holds the manipulators", perform microvascular anastomoses on 2 mm PVA vessel models visualized through the VITOM 3D exoscope on a 32" 3D/4K display. Motion scaling was set to x10, and micro-dilator and micro-needle holder suture cut NanoWrist instruments were used, with footswitch control of instrumentation. In the trial, 13 participants each performed nine anastomoses across three sessions, yielding 117 anastomoses for analysis.
requirements: Requires the Symani Surgical System cart with macropositioner and micromanipulators, the VITOM 3D exoscope with 3D polarized glasses, artificial 2 mm PVA vessels, and 8-0 nylon microsurgical sutures
constraints: Studied only in a preclinical training environment on artificial vessel models, with participants who had no prior experience using the surgical robotic system
target_learning_goals: robotic-assisted microsurgical anastomosis technique
handling of the Symani Surgical System
examples: Participants performed three anastomoses per session with six sutures each, with time recorded from picking up the suture to cutting the last suture

article_title: Designing a synthetic simulator to teach open surgical skills for limb exploration in trauma: a qualitative study exploring the experiences and perspectives of educators and surgical trainees.
citation: Heskin L., Simms C., Traynor O., Galvin R. (2021). Designing a synthetic simulator to teach open surgical skills for limb exploration in trauma: a qualitative study exploring the experiences and perspectives of educators and surgical trainees. BMC Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12893-021-01417-7
title: Synthetic full task trainer for limb exploration in trauma
description: A proposed synthetic full task trainer for teaching open limb exploratory procedures in trauma, designed from stakeholder requirements gathered in this study. Participants specified that "the physicality of the simulator needs to look and feel real", with injured structures in context among uninjured muscles, vessels and nerves, pulsatile bleeding capability, replaceable parts, and materials that react like real tissue. It is viewed as most suitable for mid-level registrars in plastic, orthopaedic and vascular surgery and for team use.
requirements: A content expert who knows the critical steps, danger points and consequences of errors must be part of the design team
Instruments and consumables such as grafts should come with the kit, with a detailed instructional video and easy-plugin technology
Replaceable parts or removable modules to keep running costs low
constraints: Most synthetic offerings with simulated blood vessels under the skin are prohibitively expensive
May be less relevant for senior surgeons unless complexity increases
Multiple scenarios in one simulator makes a more complex design
target_learners: surgical trainees, particularly mid-level registrars in plastic, orthopaedic and vascular surgery
target_learning_goals: open surgical skills for limb exploration and repair in trauma
decision-making for complex limb injuries
examples: Participants suggested pulsatile bleeding, clamping the artery, diathermy use, anastomosis checking, ischemic skin edges, bone fragments with matching simulated imaging, and moving fingers to test tendon repairs

article_title: Exploring pooled analysis of pretested items to monitor the performance of medical students exposed to different curriculum designs.
citation: Hamamoto Filho PT, Lourenção PLTA, Abbade JF, Cecílio-Fernandes D, Caramori JT, Bicudo AM. (2021). Exploring pooled analysis of pretested items to monitor the performance of medical students exposed to different curriculum designs. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0257293
title: Systems-based integrated preclinical curriculum with a structured humanities and community-based axis
description: The new curriculum implemented in 2019 at BMS-UNESP replaced the traditional three-cycle, subject-based design with two cycles: a pre-clinical cycle (years 1–3) and a clerkship (years 4–6). Basic sciences were taught using a systems-based approach, integrating traditional subjects into courses such as one on the "cell" and one on the "nervous system". Social sciences disciplines previously taught independently were organized along a structured axis for the humanities, including interdisciplinary and community-based approaches.

Organization of social sciences disciplines along a structured humanities axis
constraints: The article notes the new design (3-3) was innovative in Brazil, where the 2-2-2 format is most common

early contact with community and humanities perspectives
examples: Traditional subjects of cellular biology, biochemistry, hematology were integrated into a course on the cell; neuroanatomy, physiology, embryology, and neurology were integrated into a course on the nervous system

citation: Melillo Robert, Leisman Gerry, Mualem Raed, Ornai Alon, Carmeli Eli. (2020). Persistent Childhood Primitive Reflex Reduction Effects on Cognitive, Sensorimotor, and Academic Performance in ADHD. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2020.431835
title: Synchronized metronome training (SMT) computer-based timing system
description: SMT is "a computer-based system that trains individuals to match varying beats". Participants wore a headset, attended to a recurring metronomic beat, and performed movements such as hand-to-hand clapping with a palm sensor, receiving auditory tones and "a visual reading of millisecond latency" on a computer screen. The exercise aimed to decrease average synchronization error and improve timing/rhythmicity.

target_learners: individuals with ADHD with timing/rhythmicity deficits (in this study, ages 3.2 to 22.04 years)
target_learning_goals: timing/rhythmicity — reducing latency between the metronome beat and the participant's expectancy response
examples: In the study, participants engaged in approximately 25,000 motoric repetitions across the 12-week intervention

article_title: The Symbolic Meaning of HIV: Understanding Lecturers' Ambivalence over Teaching HIV to Dietetic Students.
citation: Mutiara Tirta Prabandari Lintang Kusuma, Kidd Tandalayo, Muturi Nancy, Procter Sandra Butin, Yarrow Linda, Hsu Wei-Wen. (2020). The Symbolic Meaning of HIV: Understanding Lecturers’ Ambivalence over Teaching HIV to Dietetic Students. Journal of the International Association of Providers of AIDS Care. https://doi.org/10.1177/2325958220939755
title: The symbolic meaning of HIV as a restricted area for dietetic students, shaped by past restricted access and cultural-religious conformity
description: Using symbolic interactionism, the authors conclude that among Indonesian dietetic lecturers "HIV is regarded as a restricted area for dietitians." Two underlying factors produce this meaning: lecturers' own past lack of access to comprehensive HIV information, which they reproduce by limiting professional development and research; and adherence to cultural and religious values, under which sex is a taboo topic and conformity to social norms makes teaching about HIV symbolize one's moral character. These restrictions are then imposed on students' access to HIV resources.
requirements: Understanding requires focusing on how individuals perceived HIV-related events, not on the symbols or events themselves, per the article's symbolic interactionist stance
constraints: Grounded in 13 lecturers across 3 Indonesian universities; the article states one must not seek generalization from a qualitative study
target_learning_goals: explaining how symbolic meanings and cultural norms shape teaching conduct around stigmatized health topics
examples: Lecturers reproduced the curriculum design they experienced in their own training, refused to discuss HIV outside clinical contexts, and prevented clerkship contact with HIV-positive patients

article_title: SimLife model: introducing a new teaching device in endocrine surgery simulation.
citation: Donatini G., Bakkar S., Leclere F. M., Dib W., Suaud S., Oriot D., Breque C., Richer J. P., Faure J. P., Danion J. (2020). SimLife model: introducing a new teaching device in endocrine surgery simulation. Updates in Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s13304-020-00871-x
title: Classification of surgical simulators into synthetic and organic categories
description: The article presents a two-branch taxonomy of surgical simulators: synthetic simulators (plastic, rubber or latex-based, virtual reality, and computer-based) and organic simulators, subdivided into animal- and human-based models. It states that "the main drawback of synthetic simulators is that they lack realistic resemblance to living beings", while organic models provide high-fidelity environments but face restrictive country-specific measures; human cadaver-based models are considered the best for surgical training but are static, which perfused dynamic models such as SimLife overcome.
requirements: Organic simulators require bodies or animals and are subject to restrictive measures that vary from one country to another
constraints: Static cadaveric models do not provide real-time dynamic in-theater clinical scenarios; the taxonomy is presented in the discussion as background framing rather than a tested result
target_learning_goals: Selecting appropriate simulator types for surgical skills training
examples: SimLife is positioned as an organic dynamic simulator offering the highest possible degree of resemblance to reality, away from the patient

article_title: Should the PBL tutor be present? A cross-sectional study of group effectiveness in synchronous and asynchronous settings.
citation: Edelbring Samuel, Alehagen Siw, Mörelius Evalotte, Johansson AnnaKarin, Rytterström Patrik. (2020). Should the PBL tutor be present? A cross-sectional study of group effectiveness in synchronous and asynchronous settings. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-02018-3
title: Ensure PBL tutoring is synchronous; the tutor need not be physically in the room
description: This principle holds that what matters for PBL tutorial group effectiveness is the synchrony of tutoring, not its physical location. The study's conclusion is that "the tutor need not be in the actual room but can provide support in online settings as long as the tutoring is synchronous". Synchronously tutored groups, in-room or online, outperformed asynchronously consultant-tutored groups on cognitive and motivational measures, while online synchronous tutoring matched in-room tutoring.
requirements: Tutoring must occur synchronously, in real time, whether face-to-face or online
constraints: Non-randomised cross-sectional design limits causal conclusions
The online group was small (n = 17)
Results come from well-motivated advanced-level nursing students and may not generalise to bachelor-level students or longer programmes
target_learners: advanced-level specialist nursing and midwifery students in PBL programmes
target_learning_goals: maintaining cognitive and motivational effectiveness of PBL tutorial groups across campus and online settings
examples: Students met synchronously via the internet with the tutor from different locations (setting B), or in a room with an asynchronous consultant tutor commenting digitally (setting C), and the resulting TGEI scores were compared

article_title: Teaching as Brain Changing: Exploring Connections between Neuroscience and Innovative Teaching.
citation: Owens Melinda T., Tanner Kimberly D. (2017). Teaching as Brain Changing: Exploring Connections between Neuroscience and Innovative Teaching. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.17-01-0005
title: Synaptic plasticity: learning occurs primarily through changes in the strength and number of connections between existing neurons
description: The article presents synaptic plasticity as the core neurobiological mechanism of learning and memory: rather than new neurons, learning occurs because frequently coactivated neurons strengthen their connections, summarized as 'Neurons that fire together, wire together.' Short-term changes include inserting more neurotransmitter receptors; long-term changes include growth of new synapses that can provide a neural substrate for long-term memory. The article uses this framework to interpret why active teaching techniques promote durable learning.
requirements: Repeated coactivation of two neurons for new synapses to persist and support long-term memory
constraints: Neurogenesis contributes little: newly born neurons represent only ∼0.004% of the total population of neurons at any given time
target_learning_goals: long-term memory formation and retrieval of course content
examples: The article reanalyzes the think–pair–share as engaging synaptic plasticity: attention and motivation promote plasticity, peer discussion practices skills, and the low-stakes communal format reduces cortisol that would impede plasticity

article_title: Use of simulation-based medical training in Swiss pediatric hospitals: a national survey.
citation: Stocker M, Laine K, Ulmer F. (2017). Use of simulation-based medical training in Swiss pediatric hospitals: a national survey. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-0940-1
title: Design SBMT within a systematic curriculum-development approach including needs assessment, goals and evaluation with feedback
description: The article recommends applying the framework of Kern for curriculum development — needs assessment, educational and implementation strategies, evaluation and feedback — to simulation-based medical training. It argues that "the evaluation of any training program is an essential component to ensure feedback and maintain quality" and that in the absence of a systematic approach the risk of erratic training content increases. Only a minority of surveyed units applied such a systematic approach, which the authors identify as a shortcoming.
requirements: Needs assessment, determination of goals and objectives, and evaluation involving feedback, described as mandatory steps for any high-quality curriculum development
constraints: The article notes a lack of resources may inhibit implementation of a systematic approach, given the paucity of structured evaluation among high-penetration hospitals
target_learners: midwives and allied health professionals in pediatric hospitals
target_learning_goals: technical clinical skills
non-technical team skills
patient safety behaviors
examples: The survey assessed systematic approach via training embedded within an educational curriculum, structured participant evaluation, and research activities, finding 19 of 24 units not curriculum-embedded and 16 of 24 not evaluated
